howto.name: Meet the basic requirements
howto.text: Be at least 18 with a high school diploma or equivalent and a U.S. Social Security number.

howto.name: Complete the 63-hour pre-license course
howto.text: Finish Florida's state-approved 63-hour sales associate pre-license course and pass its end-of-course exam.

howto.name: Get fingerprinted
howto.text: Submit electronic fingerprints through a state-approved vendor for your background check.

howto.name: Apply to the DBPR
howto.text: Apply to the Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation and receive your exam authorization.

howto.name: Pass the Florida state exam
howto.text: Pass the 100-question Florida sales associate exam (75% or higher) at a Pearson VUE testing center.

howto.name: Activate your license under a broker
howto.text: Join a licensed Florida broker, such as Adams, Cameron & Co., to activate your license and start working.

Orange City is a growing, family-oriented city in west Volusia County, best known for Blue Spring State Park, a major spring-fed swimming area and manatee refuge, and for its SunRail commuter-rail stop connecting residents to Orlando. It sits between DeLand and DeBary, and offers a more affordable alternative to the coast for families and first-time buyers. Here’s exactly how to get licensed, and what the local market looks like for a new agent.

How do you get a real estate license in Orange City?

You earn the Florida real estate sales associate license, valid statewide. There is no separate Orange City license. Be 18+ with a high school diploma, complete the 63-hour pre-license course, get fingerprinted, apply to the DBPR, pass the state exam (75% to pass), and activate under a broker. Most people finish in two to four months. Full detail is in our Florida licensing guide.

Is Orange City a good market for a new real estate agent?

Yes, especially for an agent who wants an affordable, family-oriented suburb with its own real identity rather than just a bedroom community. Orange City is anchored by Blue Spring State Park, one of Florida’s best-known natural springs and manatee refuges, and by its SunRail stop, which gives residents a genuine commuter connection into Orlando. That mix, affordability, a signature natural attraction, and transit access, keeps drawing families priced out of the coast. Across Volusia County, roughly 900 homes sell each month at about a $343,000 median, and Orange City’s relative affordability keeps demand steady.

Why Blue Spring State Park defines Orange City’s identity

Blue Spring State Park, just west of Orange City, is the area’s most significant natural landmark and a major draw for tourists, residents, and real estate interest. The park protects the largest spring on the St. Johns River and serves as one of Florida’s premier winter refuge sites for West Indian Manatees. From mid-November through March, the spring’s constant 72-degree water attracts hundreds of manatees seeking warmth, creating one of the Southeast’s most accessible wildlife-viewing experiences. The park was acquired by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection in 1972 specifically to establish manatee protections, and the results have been dramatic: from roughly 14 documented manatees in the early 1970s to a record 729 in 2023. For agents, this matters because Blue Spring transforms Orange City from a generic suburb into a genuine destination with year-round tourism, seasonal economic activity, and families who choose the area deliberately for its natural character. Buyers here often ask about proximity to the park, the seasonal rhythm, and the small-town identity that comes with a real, protected landmark.

Orange City’s award-winning spring water legacy

Orange City’s story is inseparable from Blue Spring. In the 1880s, prospector and orange grower Louis Thursby purchased the spring and operated Blue Spring Landing as a steamboat hub, shipping tourists and cargo throughout Florida’s waterways. The city’s reputation for spring water quality was so established that Orange City won an important award for its water at the 1904 St. Louis Exposition, cementing the town’s identity around natural resources and quality. That heritage shapes how Orange City presents itself today: not as a random suburb, but as a place with genuine history and a real geographic advantage. Agents who understand this narrative, one built on intentional development around a genuine geographic asset rather than arbitrary expansion, have a stronger conversation with buyers seeking character-driven communities.

Orange City’s rapid growth and stable family market

Orange City’s population has grown meaningfully since the 2020 census, expanding roughly 24% in five years while continuing to grow at nearly 4% annually. The median age of 44.2 years skews slightly older than coastal towns, reflecting a mix of established families and retirees seeking affordability and authentic small-town character without the intensity of resort communities. Retail Trade, Healthcare & Social Assistance, and Educational Services anchor local employment, pointing to a stable, year-round economic base independent of seasonal tourism swings. This employment profile creates steady, non-volatile real estate activity rather than the boom-bust cycles of purely vacation-driven markets. For new agents, that consistency is a real advantage: predictable buyer flow, fewer market shocks, and a more forgiving learning curve.

Winter manatee season and Orange City’s market rhythm

From mid-November through March, Blue Spring State Park restricts water activities to protect the winter manatee population, and that seasonal closure creates a distinctive market pattern for agents. Fall sees a surge of seasonal visitors and relocation inquiries as tourists discover Blue Spring, and spring brings renewed buyer momentum as weather warms. Winter rental demand spikes among visitors drawn to the park, opening a secondary niche for agents who specialize in seasonal income properties. Understanding these seasonal rhythms, buyer flow, and inventory timing gives agents who work Orange City a real edge over generalists. It’s a specific, small expertise, but genuine and valuable.

Does the brokerage you start with matter?

More than the town you pick. Your license must be held by a broker, and that brokerage decides your training, tools, and support in the make-or-break first year. A recognized local name carries real weight. Sellers trust it before you say a word.

Why start your real estate career with Adams, Cameron & Co.?

Adams, Cameron & Co. has been the area’s largest brokerage since 1963, with a West Volusia office just minutes away in DeLand and around 300 agents across Volusia and Flagler County. New agents get in-house marketing at no cost, seven-day non-competing manager support, structured training, and the global Leading Real Estate Companies of the World referral network.

What is your next step?

Read the licensing guide, see the neighborhoods worth knowing in our Orange City neighborhood guide, go deeper on the town’s real story in our full history of Orange City, then start a conversation with Adams, Cameron & Co. No pressure, just a clear picture of the path.
